title: Indian-American Author Neal Bakshi Says He Was Detained at US Border After Greenland Holiday
excerpt: The entrepreneur and US citizen, who holds Global Entry clearance, described being pulled into a windowless room with other people of colour and questioned about his affiliations.
body:
• Neal Bakshi, an Indian-American author and entrepreneur born and raised in the US, says he was detained at the border after returning from a holiday in Greenland.
  • Despite holding Global Entry — a trusted-traveller programme meant to speed up border re-entry — Bakshi was pulled aside for what officers called a "random" selection.
  • He described being taken to a windowless room where all the people waiting were people of colour, and later moved to a smaller room for interrogation about his personal affiliations.
  • The incident has reignited debate about racial profiling at US ports of entry amid the ongoing immigration enforcement crackdown.

What Happened at the Border

Neal Bakshi, the son of Indian immigrants and a lifelong American citizen, says what should have been an ordinary journey home turned into a deeply unsettling experience. Returning to the United States from a holiday in Greenland, Bakshi — an author, entrepreneur and founder of Awaken Mind Sciences — was stopped by border officers despite being enrolled in Global Entry, the US Customs and Border Protection programme designed to expedite clearance for pre-approved, low-risk travellers.

https://x.com/DropSiteNews/status/2097795090492072310

An officer told him he had been "randomly selected" for further questioning, according to Bakshi, who shared the account in an Instagram video that has since drawn widespread attention.

"The agents would not reveal to me why I was being taken to the back for processing until the very end of the encounter. They took me to a large waiting area where other people, only of colour, were waiting to be processed."

— Neal Bakshi

Inside the Windowless Room

Bakshi described being led to a large waiting area filled exclusively with people of colour. From there, he was moved to a smaller room for more intensive questioning. He said the physical environment added to his distress — damaged seating, a bathroom without a lock, and sallow yellow lighting in a windowless space.

Officers asked for every piece of personal information and interrogated him about his affiliations with certain groups, he said. He was ultimately told the questioning was "for his own safety."

Bakshi acknowledged that secondary screening was not entirely unfamiliar — he said he has been "randomly" selected for additional checks since he was a teenager. But this encounter, he said, felt fundamentally different in its intensity and the conditions of detention.

A Pattern of Scrutiny

The incident comes against the backdrop of an intensified immigration enforcement regime under the current administration. Indian-origin travellers and residents have reported heightened scrutiny at ports of entry and within the country, from secondary screenings at airports to Immigration and Customs Enforcement operations at domestic transit points.

Earlier reports documented ICE expanding its presence at US airports, creating new risks even for legal visa holders on domestic flights. Indian students have also reported leaving US universities in record numbers as the broader visa environment tightens.

For Bakshi — born and raised in America, with full citizenship and trusted-traveller clearance — the experience raises a pointed question about who gets treated as a stranger at the border and why.

What It Means for the Diaspora

The episode has resonated widely within Indian-American communities, where anxieties about profiling have risen alongside the broader crackdown. Bakshi was eventually allowed to leave, but the questions his account raises are not easily dismissed. If a US citizen with Global Entry clearance can be pulled into a windowless room for intensive questioning on what appears to be a routine re-entry, the promise of trusted-traveller programmes is undermined for millions of Americans who happen to have brown skin.

US Customs and Border Protection has not publicly commented on Bakshi's specific case. The agency has previously maintained that secondary screenings are conducted randomly and do not target individuals based on race or ethnicity.

Looking Ahead

Bakshi's account is likely to fuel ongoing congressional scrutiny of border enforcement practices and their impact on minority citizens. Civil rights organisations have called for greater transparency around how "random" selections are made and whether algorithmic or human biases play a role in who gets flagged for additional screening.
nri_angle: An Indian-American citizen's border detention despite Global Entry clearance has heightened fears of racial profiling among Indian diaspora travellers.
